title: Autoencoders & variational autoencoders
summary: An autoencoder reconstructs inputs through a bottleneck; a VAE learns a distribution over latent variables.
why: Regularizing latent distributions supports sampling and smoother latent organization.
interview: Derive the ELBO and explain why reparameterization permits encoder gradients.
derivation: The random epsilon is sampled independently of encoder parameters. Gradients therefore pass through the deterministic map from mu and log-variance to z.

A deterministic autoencoder only constrains observed encoded points; unvisited latent regions can decode poorly. A VAE regularizes toward a prior but can still suffer posterior collapse. Reconstruction loss follows the decoder likelihood, not a universally correct MSE.

steps.note: Two heads parameterize a diagonal Gaussian.
Choose Bernoulli/Gaussian or another justified observation model.
Sum feature dimensions before averaging batch consistently.
steps.transformation: Sum feature reconstruction NLL + diagonal Gaussian KL

traps: A powerful decoder may ignore z, causing posterior collapse.
Mixing mean reconstruction with summed KL silently changes their relative weight.
Variance and standard deviation are different quantities.
tradeoff: Larger KL weight enforces the prior more strongly but can reduce reconstruction fidelity.
code:
import torch

mu = torch.zeros(4, 8)
logvar = torch.zeros_like(mu)
z = mu + torch.exp(0.5 * logvar) * torch.randn_like(mu)
kl = -0.5 * (1 + logvar - mu.square() - logvar.exp()).sum(-1).mean()
assert z.shape == (4, 8) and kl.item() == 0.0

explanations.title: A bottleneck versus a distribution over latent variables
paragraphs: A deterministic autoencoder maps x to z and reconstructs x from z. Reconstruction loss constrains encoded training points, but arbitrary gaps between those points need not decode to plausible samples. A low-dimensional bottleneck alone does not guarantee a smooth generative distribution.

A VAE encoder produces mu and log-variance [B,Dz], defining a diagonal Gaussian q(z|x). The decoder defines p(x|z), and a prior such as a unit Gaussian defines where generation samples latent vectors.

At training time sample z from the approximate posterior; at generation time sample from the prior. Decoding only the posterior mean tests reconstruction behavior and does not evaluate unconditional sampling quality.
explanations.flow:
x -> encoder -> mu, logvar
epsilon ~ N(0,I) -> z = mu + exp(0.5*logvar)*epsilon
z -> decoder -> parameters of p(x|z)

explanations.title: ELBO, reparameterization, and the sign of the loss
paragraphs: Insert q(z|x) into log p(x) and apply Jensen to obtain an expected log-likelihood minus KL(q||p). Maximizing this ELBO is equivalent to minimizing negative reconstruction log-likelihood plus a KL penalty.

Sample epsilon independently of encoder parameters, then compute z=mu+sigma*epsilon. The randomness is isolated in epsilon, while gradients pass through mu and sigma. With logvar=log(sigma^2), sigma=exp(0.5*logvar), not exp(logvar).

For a diagonal Gaussian and standard normal prior, KL has a closed form summed over latent dimensions. Reconstruction reduction must be explicit: summing pixels and averaging batches produces a different scale from averaging every scalar. That scale changes the effective KL weight.

explanations.title: Reconstruction likelihood and posterior collapse
paragraphs: For Bernoulli pixels use an appropriate binary log-likelihood; for a Gaussian observation model, squared error corresponds to assumptions about observation variance. Choosing MSE just because the input is an image leaves the likelihood assumption unstated.

If mu=0 and logvar=0, the approximate posterior matches the unit Gaussian and KL is zero. That is desirable only if the latent still conveys useful information. A powerful decoder can ignore z, causing posterior collapse despite reasonable reconstructions.

Inspect reconstruction and KL terms separately, per-dimension activity, and prior samples. A beta coefficient changes the rate-distortion trade-off; values other than one generally change the standard ELBO objective rather than merely accelerating the same optimization.
